Among Us
uh-MUNG US
proper noun (Gen Alpha slang)
Among Us, a social-deduction game by the small studio Innersloth, released in June 2018 and suddenly huge in the late summer and fall of 2020, when streamers and housebound students played it nightly. Up to fifteen bean-shaped crewmates do tasks on a spaceship while one to three secret Impostors sabotage and kill; players call emergency meetings, argue, and vote someone out ("ejected"). It gave Gen Z and Gen Alpha the words sus, vent, ejected, emergency meeting, and the meme amogus.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Among Us is the game where a few players are secret "impostors" and everyone else must figure out who. Kids accuse each other ("Red is sus!"), defend themselves, and vote people off the ship. The Christian observation: the game is a cartoon of something Scripture takes very seriously — the betrayer among friends. At the Last Supper Jesus said, "one of you shall betray me" (Mat 26:21), and the disciples did not point at each other; they "began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?" (Mat 26:22). Among Us trains the opposite reflex: suspect everyone but yourself. Bluffing in a game everyone agreed to play is not the sin of lying, but the habits around it matter. Scripture forbids the careless accusation: "Thou shalt not raise a false report" (Exo 23:1); it demands hearing both sides: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Pro 18:17); and it commands the hardest examination to start at home: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" (2Co 13:5). A father can tell a five-year-old: "In that game people pretend to be tricky and others have to guess. In real life we don’t accuse people unless we’re sure, and we always ask Jesus to check our own hearts first."

Webster 1828 Definition

Innersloth’s social-deduction game (2018; viral 2020) of crewmates and secret impostors — a cartoon of the betrayer among friends, which trains suspicion of others where the disciples asked, "Lord, is it I?"

AMONG US, proper n. (Innersloth, 2018; viral 2020) The spaceship game of crewmates, secret impostors, meetings, and votes. "Let’s play Among Us — I call Red."

Vocabulary it spread: sus, impostor, crewmate, vent, ejected, emergency meeting, amogus (meme distortion of the title).

Decode for parents: mild cartoon violence; the moral content is in the bluffing and accusing.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:21 — "And as they did eat, he said, Verily I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me."

Mat 26:22 — "And they were exceeding sorrowful, and began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?"

Exo 23:1 — "Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness."

Pro 18:17 — "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him."

2Co 13:5 — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates ?"

Modern Corruption

Among Us rehearses the hunt for a betrayer and rewards quick accusation; Scripture forbids the false report, requires hearing the neighbor, and turns the search inward — "Lord, is it I?"

expand to see more

Agreed-upon bluffing games are old — Mafia, Werewolf, poker — and the deception inside them is a convention all the players accept. The concern with Among Us is less the bluff than the accusation culture it fed: "sus" became a word children throw at each other in real classrooms, and the vote-off became a playground ritual of exclusion. A game can train a reflex of suspicion that outlives the round.

Turn the game toward the Upper Room. The disciples, told that a traitor sat among them, examined themselves before they examined anyone else. Teach that order: check my own heart first, hear the other side, never raise a false report. A child who learns it from a bean-shaped spaceman has learned something many adults have not.
